sourceAnchors.claimSupported: C03: core vs system integration boundary

actions.text: If you want a RISC-V processor design that you can study, modify and integrate into a system, CVA6 offers a concrete starting point. It is a configurable open-source processor-IP family, with 32-bit and 64-bit variants sharing SystemVerilog source. IP means a reusable hardware design: the core executes instructions, while memory, peripherals and software complete the system. We will see embedded control, Linux hosting and accelerator management. Those uses are possibilities supported by specific configurations and platforms. They are not guarantees for every variant. This overview answers three questions: what is CVA6, how does it process instructions, and where can you learn more? By the end, you should be able to distinguish a core from a system, read a configuration example, and identify the evidence needed for a capability claim. I created this community course for OpenHW Explorer, interpreting official documentation and project records. Detailed architecture and verification topics are left for later lessons.

actions.text: Place these names at different levels. RISC-V is an instruction-set architecture: it defines instructions and their software-visible behavior. OpenHW organizes collaboration around open hardware, and CORE-V is its portfolio of open cores and companion projects. CVA6 is one processor-core family implementing RISC-V. Following the diagram, parameters define a particular configuration; platform hardware and software then turn it into a system. CV64A6 evolved from Ariane, developed at ETH Zürich and the University of Bologna. RV32 was added later. The ISA, portfolio, core and development board therefore describe different objects. The Foundation and CORE-V naming courses provide more background on the organization and its terminology.

scopeNotes: PMP provides access protection configured through dedicated CSRs; CSR is a broader control/status register category.
Linux here refers to a conventional paged system.
CV-X-IF is an instruction coprocessor extension interface; this page does not claim that Occamy uses it. The Occamy example illustrates manager/accelerator roles.

assets.alt: Start with the system task, then choose a configuration and platform

actions.text: Start with the system task, rather than asking which name sounds most powerful. Embedded control needs a dedicated program and platform interfaces, memory and interrupts. GPIO, UART and SPI are platform peripherals, not features automatically contained in the CVA6 core. PMP is a physical-memory protection mechanism; its settings are held in dedicated CSRs. CSR is a broader category of control and status registers, not a second independent memory-protection unit. Here, a Linux host means a conventional paged system, requiring suitable privilege modes, MMU translation and boot software. Cheshire is a named platform example. Accelerator management needs coordinating software and system interfaces. CV-X-IF extends instruction execution through a coprocessor; mentioning it does not establish that Occamy uses this interface. Occamy illustrates a CVA6 manager working with a separate Snitch accelerator. The SDK and FPGA flow are development entry points, not proof that every illustrated control application has been tested. For FPGA prototypes or ASIC integrations, configuration, platform and software must fit together. Next, compare actual parameters.

actions.text: These columns come from one pinned source snapshot. The CV32A60X example is 32-bit and machine-mode only. It has no MMU, disables the F and D floating-point extensions, and sets the PMP-entry count to zero. The RV64, Sv39 example enables translation, three privilege modes and floating-point extensions, with eight PMP entries. M, S and U mean machine, supervisor and user mode, distinguishing execution privileges. Shared source can therefore produce different feature combinations. Selecting an MMU is about address translation; enabling floating point is about the instructions software can execute. These are separate decisions, not a single advanced-core switch. You do not need to memorize the table. Ask what your software requires and what the configuration actually supplies. The explorer also offers a dual-issue example; issue width is not measured performance. The CV32A60X TRL5 release discussed later has a separate named scope. Keep that release distinct from these source examples. The right column is specifically cv64a6_imafdc_sv39, not all RV64 configurations. Zero PMP entries does not mean no system protection. Shared source does not make arbitrary combinations valid; implementation parameters alone do not establish full architectural CSR conformance.

content.qualifier: Functional view; boxes are not pipeline stages. The historical six-stage baseline does not define every configuration.
scopeNotes: This is a responsibility diagram, not a complete RTL netlist or a one-box-per-cycle/stage specification.
Execution results return to the scoreboard. Commit updates architectural registers and CSRs in program order and coordinates relevant stores/exceptions.
Load/store data requests use configured memory support and system interconnect; debug is a separate platform function.
The fetch arrow denotes access to instruction memory, with cache, translation and bus details simplified. Crossed lines without a junction marker do not denote a connection.

actions.text: Follow the instruction path across the top. The frontend selects fetch addresses and uses branch prediction to help maintain supply. Decode identifies operations and registers. Issue checks operand and execution-resource readiness, while the scoreboard tracks instructions and their results. Execution handles integer operations, branches and memory accesses, returning results to the scoreboard. Floating-point and coprocessor interfaces depend on configuration; the coprocessor itself is not built into every variant. Commit then updates architectural registers and CSRs in program order and coordinates relevant stores and exceptions. Outside the core, the platform supplies memory, interconnect, interrupts, debug and peripherals. Fetching instructions and loading program data create different traffic, using the selected memory support and platform connections. Debug is not the destination of an ordinary data request. Cache, translation and bus details are simplified, and crossed lines without a junction do not denote connections. This is a responsibility diagram, not a complete RTL netlist. The historical six-stage description refers to an original baseline; box counts specify neither stages nor cycles. Next, two instructions make the distinction between waiting and committing concrete.

scenes.title: An instruction also needs its input data to be ready

content.title: An instruction also needs its input data to be ready
content.learnerQuestion: Why can the next instruction wait even when an execution unit is free?

blocks.label: ① Read memory
blocks.text: lw x5, 0(x10) · Loads 12 in this example

blocks.label: ② Use the result
blocks.text: add x6, x5, x7 · x7 = 3 in this example

blocks.label: Dependency
blocks.text: New x5 from the load → Source operand of the add

content.qualifier: Conceptual RV32 single-issue baseline: valid aligned address, x7 ready, no exceptions or flushes; no fixed-cycle claim.
scopeNotes: This is a conceptual RV32 single-issue baseline, with no fixed-cycle claim or guarantee for every CVA6 configuration. Assume a valid word-aligned address, x7 ready, and no exceptions or flushes.
lw x5, 0(x10) reads a 32-bit word. Twelve and three are teaching assumptions, not measured data; after normal retirement, x5=12 and x6=15.

The add needs the new x5 produced by the load: a read-after-write (RAW) dependency. An idle ALU cannot supply a missing source operand. The scoreboard tracks readiness and can forward returned values.
The x5=12 on the path to the ALU is a usable operand value, not proof that the architectural register has already been updated. Forwarding can precede retirement; no fixed advance window is promised.

Both completed instructions reach the conceptual pending-commit path. Commit retires them in program order to produce the final architectural state. The dashed load path distinguishes one completion route and does not mean retirement is optional.
The memory-to-LSU arrow denotes returned data in this example; cache, bus and scoreboard-storage details are simplified. The result paths are not a complete physical netlist.
content.workedExample: RV32: x10=0x1000; the 32-bit word at that valid aligned address is 12; x7=3. After normal retirement, x5=12 and x6=15.

This is a conceptual event explorer. State numbers are not clock cycles; it is not a CVA6 simulator.

Read all five conceptual events
  1. Identify operations and dependency

    Decode identifies the load destination x5 and the add sources x5/x7. Knowing a register number does not make its new value available.

  2. Memory access in progress; add lacks data

    The load has not returned, so the new x5 needed by the add is unavailable. Even with a free integer unit, the add cannot substitute the old x5 in this example.

  3. Result 12 is ready and can be forwarded

    The load returns 12, which the scoreboard can provide to the dependent add. This marks result availability, not a claim that the load has already retired at this point.

  4. The add produces 15

    With operand and resource conditions satisfied, the add calculates 12+3=15. This conceptual state does not specify its exact cycle relationship to load retirement.

  5. Program state after normal retirement

    After both instructions retire normally, architectural x5 is 12 and x6 is 15. Commit handles architectural state; returning a result does not by itself establish retirement.

actions.text: Consider the two instructions. The load reads a 32-bit word from the address in x10, producing a new x5. The add combines that value with x7 to produce x6. Assume a valid word-aligned address, a memory value of twelve, x7 ready with value three, and no exceptions or flushes. Decode can identify register numbers before data returns, but cannot supply a result that does not exist. The add needs the new x5 from the load: a read-after-write dependency. A free integer unit cannot replace that missing operand with the old x5. In this RV32 single-issue baseline, the scoreboard tracks readiness and can forward the returned twelve. The x5 equals twelve label on the ALU input denotes an available operand, not proof that the architectural register has already changed. With the conditions satisfied, the add produces fifteen. Both completed instructions still pass through commit; after normal retirement in program order, architectural x5 is twelve and x6 is fifteen. The dashed load path does not make retirement optional. These are conceptual events, not fixed cycles or a guaranteed forwarding window. Cache and bus details are simplified. Advance the states to separate result availability from architectural-state updates.

scenes.title: Caching, address translation and physical protection have different jobs

content.title: Caching, address translation and physical protection have different jobs
content.learnerQuestion: Do caches, the MMU and PMP solve the same problem?

blocks.label: Cache
blocks.text: Which instructions or data can be reused nearby?

blocks.label: MMU
blocks.text: How are virtual addresses mapped to physical addresses and page permissions checked?

blocks.label: PMP
blocks.text: Which physical-address regions permit reads, writes or execution?

content.qualifier: MMU / Sv39, cache type and PMP-entry count depend on configuration.
scopeNotes: A cache stores and reuses instructions or data; a cache hit does not itself grant permission. This comparison does not specify exact checking timing for each hit.

The VA-to-PA/page-permission description applies when paging is enabled. Sv39 is one RV64 paging mode, not a family-wide CVA6 guarantee. Sv32 is an RV32 paging example; Bare does not perform paged translation.

PMP assigns read, write and execute permissions to physical-address regions. Enforcement depends on effective privilege, matching entries and settings; it is not an unconditional rule shared by all modes.
These are parallel responsibilities, not fixed serial Cache→MMU→PMP checkpoints. Interconnect and physical memory attributes are outside this short comparison.

The eight-PMP-entry value on the previous page is a named configuration parameter at 81245a4. It does not establish a family-wide count, verification completion or full v1.13 conformance. Architectural CSR exposure, read-only-zero slots and implementation parameters require separate checks.
content.workedExample: 'MMU enabled' and '8 PMP entries' are not interchangeable; a cache hit does not bypass permission requirements.

actions.text: Separate three questions when software accesses memory. A cache holds reusable instructions or data, helping avoid repeated accesses to more distant storage. In a paged system, the MMU uses page tables to translate virtual addresses and check page permissions. PMP controls read, write and execute permissions for physical-address regions; its effect also depends on privilege mode and settings. Our RV64, Sv39 source example includes an MMU and eight PMP entries. Those describe different capabilities. Reusing a value may avoid another distant-memory access, while mapping and permissions remain separate questions. A cache hit does not establish that an access is permitted. The parallel comparison teaches responsibilities, rather than three fixed serial hardware checkpoints. Their presence and integration must still be checked in the selected configuration and system. Sv39 is one RV64 paging mode; Sv32 is an RV32 example, while Bare does not perform paged translation. PMP needs effective-privilege, entry-matching and setting checks. Its implementation count is not a conformance conclusion.

blocks.label: Platform hardware

blocks.text: Toolchain + Platform initialization + Program / Operating system

blocks.label: SDK / Genesys2 boot example

scopeNotes: The toolchain builds binaries and is not a runtime handoff stage; match the ISA, ABI and platform. GCC/LLVM/Binutils are generic examples, while this SDK build uses its pinned dependencies.
The .dts label denotes device-tree source. Firmware normally passes a compiled binary DTB to the kernel. This SDK FIT template embeds u-boot.dtb.

ext4 is a generic root-filesystem format example, not the default format asserted for this Genesys2 SDK. Its FIT embeds a rootfs.cpio.gz initial ramdisk; the README describes kernel startup of user space from Ramdisk.

BootROM→OpenSBI→U-Boot→Linux→user programs is the Genesys2 control-handoff example at SDK 267794d. OpenSBI remains resident for M-mode services; U-Boot operates during boot. The QEMU example skips U-Boot and is not CVA6 RTL verification.

The tested configuration list is the maintainers’ statement: cv32a6_ima_sv32_fpga and cv64a6_imafdc_sv39. This course has not independently rerun boot or verification. Board, parameter and dependency changes still require compatibility checks.

The English Use arrow denotes software consuming boot assets; the Chinese startup arrow denotes assets supporting software startup. They express complementary dependency relations, not reversed control flow. Initialization/program and hardware-row links are composition/support sketches, not full physical wiring or timing.

DDR/SDRAM, AXI, PLIC, JTAG and the peripheral list are generic examples, not features guaranteed in every CVA6 or Genesys2 instance. Bare-metal/RTOS environments do not necessarily need the Linux device-tree/rootfs combination.

content.title: Maturity statements need a configuration, version and verification scope
content.learnerQuestion: How should tests, coverage and a TRL5 statement inform your understanding of maturity?

blocks.label: Verification questions
blocks.text: Test behavior · Compare with a reference · Check coverage plans · Run regressions

blocks.label: Named release
blocks.text: cv32a60x-v6.0.0 · 2025-04-23 · Publisher states TRL5

blocks.label: Explicit release scope
blocks.text: One specific configuration · OBI · No caches · 0 PMP entries · Zifencei disabled

content.qualifier: The release does not automatically cover the whole family, later changes or an integrated system.
scopeNotes: Retain TRL5 as the publisher’s scoped terminology for the named 2025 cv32a60x-v6.0.0 release. This course has not rerated or independently certified it, and makes no claim that it is the only mature configuration in 2026.

The release resolves to b1f80bd; the general verification README example is pinned at 81245a4. General review questions are not the complete release evidence package, and the master tool setup is not automatically the historical release environment.

The four groups are evidence-review questions, not a checklist proving every activity/configuration completed. Reference-model agreement is not exhaustive correctness proof; coverage plans, code/functional coverage and regression records each need target/tool context.

The pinned verification README explicitly scopes its plan flow to VCS and a configuration modifier. It does not grant every simulator identical plan/coverage support. Regressions help detect known defects reappearing, without guaranteeing they never recur.

The publisher lists OBI, no caches, zero PMP entries and disabled Zifencei. Zero PMP entries does not establish absence of all integrated-system protection, and release limits do not extend to every family member or new variant.

Adding a cache or changing interfaces/environment requires reassessing goals and evidence rather than automatically inheriting TRL5. Existing evidence may remain useful, but its original scope cannot be transferred without justification.
The bars are a conceptual coverage-plan icon, not measured percentages. The center arrow is a conditional evidence-to-statement relation, not an automatic grading or TRL-upgrade algorithm.

actions.text: Inspecting an open design is only part of assessing confidence. Tests check particular behaviors, a reference model supports comparison, a coverage plan defines goals, and regressions check for problems after changes. These activities reduce risk. Reference-model agreement is not exhaustive proof, and regression does not guarantee that defects never recur. Interpret coverage with its plan, target and tools; the pinned verif documentation scopes its coverage-plan flow to VCS. The named example is cv32a60x-v6.0.0, released on April twenty-third, 2025. The publisher states TRL5 for a specific configuration: OBI, no caches, zero PMP entries and disabled Zifencei. The release resolves to b1f80bd, while our general verification reading comes from 81245a4. The review questions are not the complete historical release report. TRL5 neither transfers automatically to the family nor represents independent certification by this course. Zero PMP entries does not exclude all system protection. A changed cache or interface requires reassessing goals and evidence. Likewise, a merged implementation does not establish which options were enabled, tests covered, or systems booted. Preserve configuration, version and evidence scope together.

content.title: Public systems demonstrate specific roles within specific evidence scopes

blocks.label: SDK / FPGA

blocks.text: CVA6 / Cheshire · Open silicon implementation · Linux boot and project measurements

blocks.text: CVA6: Linux manager core · Snitch: many-core accelerator

content.qualifier: Public maintainer / author records; not independently reproduced here, and not performance or qualification results for other systems.
scopeNotes: All chip, board, square-group and bar illustrations are conceptual, not photographs, exact board layouts, actual core counts or benchmark charts. Use the SDK’s named Genesys2/Agilex7 targets and configuration records for concrete board evidence.

Basilisk is a specific silicon implementation using the Cheshire/CVA6 system. Cheshire is already built around CVA6; the plus sign separates core and platform responsibilities rather than adding a second independent core to a complete platform.

The Basilisk authors publish Linux-boot demonstrations, silicon measurements and implementation material. This course checks those records without independently reproducing them or transferring frequency, power or qualification results to another CVA6 system.

Complete open silicon system denotes system integration/implementation flow, not that every physical asset is public. The project explicitly omits proprietary pads from its GDS download; assets retain their own availability/license boundaries.

Occamy uses a Linux-capable CVA6 management core with a Snitch-cluster-based many-core accelerator for intensive computation. The four squares are a group icon, not a four-core count; accelerator scale is not CVA6-core scale.

Task scheduling/control is a conceptual interpretation of the Linux management role, not evidence of a specific hardware scheduler or real-time guarantee. The two-way arrow denotes collaboration, not identical or symmetric execution roles.

The Basilisk footer’s 2026-10-13 is the first course research access date, rechecked on 2026-10-14. It is not a tapeout, measurement or publication date. Use natural plural/style wording such as project measurements in narration.

content.title: Follow development directions; check implementations and releases for current capability
content.learnerQuestion: How can you follow development without treating plans as delivered features?

blocks.label: Software compatibility
blocks.text: Broader software profiles and OS support

blocks.label: Cache and compute subsystems
blocks.text: Cache integration · Vector connections · Multi-core platforms

blocks.label: Reliability and verification
blocks.text: Redundancy / Hardening directions · Configuration verification · CI consistency

content.qualifier: Directions summarized from the 2026-07-15 roadmap version, not a list of delivered features.
scopeNotes: The three directions are based on the July 15, 2026 roadmap. Detailed bullets are teaching summaries, not individual official commitments or an item-by-item account of delivery status in October 2026.

Software profiles here are RISC-V ISA compatibility profiles. Concrete entries include RVB23/RVA23 objectives, Zephyr repository integration and a bare-metal SDK. They do not establish support for every mainstream OS, distribution or toolchain, or all of the expanded ecosystem bullets.

The concrete cache work concerns HPDCache/HPICache, platform integration and optional hardening. Do not generalize it to arbitrary cache hierarchies, automatic coherence or universal configuration support.

Unify the vector headings in narration as vector-support and ARA-connection work. The roadmap discusses reconnecting ARA, possibly through CV-X-IF; it does not establish existing V-extension support for every CVA6 configuration.

The multicore direction concerns platforms such as CV-TCCC/Culsans. Coordination, scheduling and software support are teaching topics, not proof of a completed hardware scheduler, real-time guarantee or fixed core count.

Redundancy and hardening concern optional cache hardening, distinct DCLS projects and convergence plans. Existing project results, ongoing verification and future work have different status; no family-wide maturity or safety-certification claim follows.
Configuration verification and CI summarize selected verification, new CI and SSoT tool-alignment activities, not complete verification of all configurations and platforms.

Named releases, merged implementations, project examples and roadmaps are the course author’s evidence-reading categories, not an official quality ladder. Categories can coexist; version, configuration, testing and system boundaries still matter.

questions.question: You plan to integrate CVA6 into an FPGA system and still need memory, an interconnect and peripherals. Which statement best describes CVA6's role?

options.label: CVA6 is the RISC-V instruction-set standard, specifying the peripherals every system must use.
CVA6 is configurable processor IP; a complete system also needs platform hardware and matching software.
CVA6 is the CVA6 SDK, mainly providing a compiler, boot firmware and Linux.
CVA6 is a fixed-configuration FPGA development board with predefined memory and peripherals.

questions.analysis: Separate the objects: the ISA defines instruction behavior; the core implements it; a configuration selects core features; the platform connects memory and peripherals; software is built and booted for that system.

optionFeedback.A: The RISC-V ISA defines software-visible instructions and behavior. CVA6 implements the ISA as processor IP; the platform determines its peripherals.
optionFeedback.B: Correct. The core, its configuration, the platform and software have different roles. Reusable core IP does not include every part of the system.
optionFeedback.C: The SDK is a companion project for building software for named targets. It is distinct from the CVA6 hardware core that executes the software.
optionFeedback.D: CVA6 can be integrated into different FPGA or ASIC systems. A board is a specific platform, not the definition of the processor-IP family.

questions.question: In the lesson's single-issue baseline example, lw x5, 0(x10) is followed by add x6, x5, x7. The load result for x5 is not yet available, while the integer execution unit is free. Why can the add still not issue?

options.label: Because the add must use the load/store unit to read the memory address of x5.
Because decode cannot yet identify the add's source registers.
Because the add's operand can become available only after the load retires.
Because it needs the new x5 produced by the load; both operand readiness and execution-resource readiness are required.

questions.analysis: The example assumes x7 is ready and omits exceptions, branch flushes and other stalls. It tests identification and readiness of operands, not cycle counting, and does not generalize this older baseline description to every configuration.

optionFeedback.A: The add uses register operands. It is waiting for the x5 value produced by the load; the add itself is not reading memory.
optionFeedback.B: Its source registers can already be identified from the instruction. Knowing that x5 is needed differs from having its new value available.
optionFeedback.C: In this baseline, a result can be forwarded through the scoreboard before the architectural register is updated. Result availability differs from retirement; the relevant condition is operand readiness.
optionFeedback.D: Correct. A free execution unit satisfies the resource condition but not the data dependency. Once the load result is available, the add has the operand it needs in this example.

questions.question: You want to reproduce an existing CVA6 Linux software flow before moving to your own board. Which basis for choosing a target is strongest?

options.label: Check the SDK's listed tested configurations, boards and matching hardware/software versions, then select a target.
Choose RV64 alone; 64-bit width establishes that every requirement for booting Linux is present.
Choose any configuration with a cache; a cache can replace the MMU and boot firmware.
Choose the CV32A60X TRL5 release alone; its maturity statement proves that the SDK has tested it as a Linux target.

questions.analysis: Start from a traceable target and evaluate changes afterward. The SDK's tested-target list is the maintainers' record; this course has not rerun the boot experiment. Do not extend this question into an absolute claim that every Linux variant requires an MMU.

optionFeedback.A: Correct. The SDK lists both RV32/Sv32 and RV64/Sv39 targets. The evidence includes the configuration, platform and boot software; the name alone is insufficient.
optionFeedback.B: Width does not establish the MMU, privilege features, platform hardware, firmware or matching software build. A selected RV64 target still needs this evidence.
optionFeedback.C: Caches, address translation and boot software have different roles. A cache does not establish the features or complete software flow needed by a conventional paged Linux system.
optionFeedback.D: The TRL5 release and the SDK's tested Linux targets are different evidence. That named release does not replace configuration, board and software compatibility records.

options.label: The new system still uses the CVA6 name, so it can directly inherit the release's TRL5 statement.
Caches can improve performance, so the changes also prove that the system has reached a higher maturity level.
The release states TRL5 for its named configuration; the new variant needs its own configuration, verification scope and system-test evidence.
The roadmap mentions cache development, so it already provides final verification results for this new system.

questions.analysis: The cv32a60x-v6.0.0 notes cover one specific configuration, including OBI, no caches and no PMP entries. The publisher's TRL5 statement is neither a family-wide certification nor automatic coverage of a modified system.

optionFeedback.A: The name does not preserve the configuration or interface. The release explicitly covers a specific configuration; cache and interface changes alter the scope to be assessed.
optionFeedback.B: Performance goals and verification maturity require different evidence. A cache introduces behavior to verify; its presence does not establish maturity.
optionFeedback.C: Correct. The release can be cited as an existing project result, while changes and the evidence supporting new conclusions must be stated explicitly.
optionFeedback.D: The roadmap describes plans and directions. It does not report tests, coverage or acceptance results for the new system in this question.

scopeNotes: The four learning paths are Alex Chen’s course recommendations, not an officially certified or separately published course. Treat the original official reading paths wording as source entry points; the displayed footer explicitly attributes the arrangement to this course.

Separate the user manual’s IP/configuration scope from design documentation’s internal modules. Work-in-progress sections, historical six-stage baselines and placeholder chapters are not complete guides for every configuration.

Start with an SDK-listed board/configuration and matching versions. Learners should record their own environment, commands, build/boot logs and failures. Reproduction records is a next action, not a claim that this course independently ran the flow.

Choose verification targets and tools first. The pinned verif README’s coverage-plan workflow is VCS-specific; do not promise identical operation with Verilator or interpret the bars as measured coverage.

Start with documentation, a small reproduction or test improvement after reading the target repository’s current contribution guide and applicable requirements. No submission/contact is automated, acceptance is not promised, and membership is not presented as compulsory.

The original English credit became Original Course. Do not carry that footer into final rendering: use the exact signature Alex Chen . OpenHW Explorer 原创课程 and real source links under both image bodies. Original PNGs remain unchanged; downloads are original v1 assets.

actions.text: You now have a map: CVA6 is configurable RISC-V core IP; configuration selects features, platform and software make a runnable system, and conclusions need suitable evidence. Choose a path by interest. For architecture, read the Introduction for IP and configuration boundaries, then the design modules, tracing data for one instruction. Historical baselines, work-in-progress sections and placeholder chapters are not complete guides to every variant. For systems, start with an SDK-listed board and configuration, match versions, and record your environment, commands, build and boot logs, including failures. That is your next experiment, not one already completed by this course. For verification, read the verif README and choose targets and tools. Separate tests, coverage plans and regression; its VCS-specific coverage-plan flow is not a promise of identical operation in other tools. Before contributing, read the repository’s current guide and choose documentation, a small reproduction or a test improvement. Preserve versions when sources disagree. The links lead to official materials, while these learning paths are my course recommendations, not an officially certified course. A small optional exercise is to find an MMU or PMP field and explain it in one configuration- and version-scoped sentence.
